title: Rotting Oranges
statement: Given a grid where each cell is 0 (fresh orange), 1 (rotten orange) or 2 (empty), return the minimum number of minutes in which no fresh orange exists. Rot spreads to the four adjacent cells every minute. Return -1 if this is impossible.

examples.explanation: The fresh orange at the bottom middle is four cells away from the nearest rotten orange.
A fresh orange with no rotten neighbour can never rot.

hints.content: The question asks for the distance to the nearest rotten orange, for every cell at once. Which traversal answers that?
Every rotten orange is a source with time 0, and rot spreads one cell per minute.
Multi-source BFS: put all rotten oranges in the queue first, then expand level by level. Each level is one minute.
After BFS, if any 0 remains, the answer is -1 because that orange can never be reached.

pseudocode: for each cell in this level of the queue:
for each of its four neighbours:
rot it and add it to the next level
return -1 if any fresh orange remains, otherwise the last minute counted
invariant: At the start of each level, every cell in the queue was reached at exactly the same minute, so BFS always expands the earliest unprocessed rot first.
whyThisPattern: Every cell needs its distance to the nearest source, which is precisely what multi-source BFS computes. The grid edges all cost one minute, so BFS level equals minute, and DFS would be the wrong tool because it does not guarantee the shortest distance.
bruteForce: Run a separate BFS from every rotten orange, or scan forward and backward repeatedly to simulate minutes: both are much slower than one BFS from all sources at once. A minute by minute simulation also needs up to m * n passes.
interviewExplanation: I start a BFS from every rotten orange at once, so all sources begin at minute zero. Each BFS level then corresponds to one minute of rot spreading, and I convert fresh neighbours of the current level into rotten cells. If any fresh orange survives the traversal it is unreachable and the answer is minus one, otherwise the number of levels is the answer.
commonMistakes: Seeding the queue with only one rotten orange instead of all of them.
Rotting neighbours of cells that were queued but not yet processed, which shortens the answer by one minute.
Returning the number of processed levels even when fresh oranges remain, instead of -1.

payload.prompt: One fresh orange is left. What is the minimum minutes?
payload.explanation: Its distance to the nearest rotten orange at the start is four steps, so it rots after four minutes.

animationSteps.title: BFS level equals minute
animationSteps.text: BFS expanded four levels, and each level corresponds to one minute of spreading.

animationSteps.title: Answer is four
animationSteps.text: All oranges rotted after four minutes, so the answer is 4.

animationSteps.title: The -1 case
animationSteps.description: A fresh orange with no rotten neighbour can never rot.
animationSteps.text: For the grid 0, 2 the fresh orange has no rotten neighbour, so it is unreachable and the answer is -1.

payload.lesson: Multi-source BFS answers shortest distance; unreachable cells are the only failure case.

options: A grid where each cell is fresh, rotten or empty
A single rotten orange and its position
A list of orange positions with timestamps
breakdown.explanation: One grid with three cell states, and empties are neither fresh nor rotten. Empty cells never need to be rotted or counted.

options: The minutes until no fresh orange remains, or -1
The count of oranges that rotted
breakdown.explanation: A time, not a set. Every rotten cell starts spreading simultaneously, so the answer is how long until the last fresh one is reached.

breakdown.prompt: Why does the search have to start from every rotten orange at once?
options: Because rot spreads outward one step per minute from all of them
Because rotten oranges are sorted by position
Because only the first one spreads
breakdown.explanation: Rot advances one cell per minute from every rotten orange at the same time, so the arrival time at any cell is its distance from the nearest rotten one. Growing outward level by level gets every cell's time at once.
